description_ru: Почему планета нагревается, какие доказательства есть у учёных и что можно сделать, чтобы замедлить потепление.
text:
Our planet has always had natural cycles of warm and cold periods, so it might seem strange to worry about the climate now. However, scientists have discovered that the present warming is happening far more quickly than anything in the past few thousand years, and that human activity is the main cause. Understanding why this is true requires a short journey into the physics of the atmosphere, and it begins with something that is actually very useful: the greenhouse effect.

Sunlight passes through the atmosphere and warms the surface of the Earth. The surface then sends some of that energy back toward space as invisible heat, which scientists call infrared radiation. Certain gases in the air, including carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour, absorb part of this heat and send some of it back down. Without this natural effect, the average temperature on Earth would be about minus eighteen degrees Celsius, and most life would not exist. The problem is not the greenhouse effect itself, but the fact that we have been making it stronger.

Since the start of the industrial revolution in the eighteenth century, people have burned enormous amounts of coal, oil and gas. When these fuels burn, they release carbon dioxide that was stored underground for millions of years. Before 1800, the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere was about 280 parts per million. Today it is above 420, the highest level in at least eight hundred thousand years, which we know from air bubbles trapped in ancient ice. Cutting down forests makes the situation worse, because trees absorb carbon dioxide as they grow.

As a result, the average global temperature has risen by about 1.1 to 1.2 degrees Celsius since the late nineteenth century. That may sound small, but the difference between today and the last ice age was only about five or six degrees. A small change in the average can shift the weather in large ways. Heat waves have become more frequent and more intense, and many of the warmest years on record have occurred in the last decade. Meanwhile, the Arctic is warming roughly three times faster than the rest of the planet.

The consequences are already visible. Glaciers in the Alps, the Himalayas and the Andes have been shrinking for decades, and the Greenland ice sheet is losing hundreds of billions of tonnes of ice every year. Because water expands when it warms and ice melts into the oceans, the global sea level has risen by around twenty centimetres since 1900, and the rise is speeding up. Low coastal areas and small island nations, which have contributed very little to the problem, are among the most threatened.

Warming also affects rainfall. A warmer atmosphere holds more water vapour, which can lead to heavier storms and floods in some regions. In others, droughts last longer, and wildfires spread more easily. Meanwhile, the oceans absorb about a quarter of our carbon dioxide emissions, which makes seawater slightly more acidic. This is a serious danger for animals with shells, and for coral reefs, which support about a quarter of all marine species, even though they cover less than one percent of the sea floor.

How do we know all this? Scientists use many independent kinds of evidence. Thermometers and weather stations have recorded temperatures for over a century, and satellites have measured the oceans, the ice and the atmosphere since the 1970s. Older information comes from tree rings, corals and layers of ice, which preserve a chemical record of past temperatures. When researchers put all of these sources together, they find the same pattern, and it matches computer models that include human emissions but not natural changes alone.

What can be done? Scientists generally agree that the most important step is to reduce emissions of greenhouse gases as fast as possible. Solar and wind power have become cheaper than coal in many countries, and electric cars are now common in several parts of the world. Governments can encourage change by putting a price on carbon, protecting forests and improving public transport. If emissions fall to net zero by about 2050, according to many climate models, the warming could be limited to around one and a half degrees.

Individual choices matter, too, although they are only part of the solution. People can save energy at home, eat less meat, fly less often and choose to cycle or walk for short trips. Perhaps just as important is talking about the issue with friends and colleagues, and voting for leaders who take it seriously. The climate has changed before, but never because of a single species. This time, the cause is us, and that means the solution is also in our hands.

questions.question: What is the greenhouse effect?
questions.answer: Gases in the air absorb heat and send some back to the surface.

questions.question: How much has the global temperature risen since the late nineteenth century?
Why is the Arctic important in the text?
questions.answer: It is warming about three times faster than the rest of the planet.

questions.answer: Reducing greenhouse gas emissions as fast as possible.
